Consequently, this yields the latter group FUn(Γ) as the result of combining two of its subgroups, specifically the subgroup generated by 2-cycle relations and the subgroup Q(Γ,M) whose embedding is geometric in nature.

Connectivity analysis between different components of complex systems is a key area of study in fields like neuroscience, climate science, and finance. Traditional frequency-domain methods have been widely used, but they fail to capture temporal relationships and often result in misleading findings, as noted by Bartsch et al. In this work, we introduce a novel time-domain approach to estimate connectivity, avoiding frequency aliasing and frequency leakage issues. The proposed method, based on the Koopman operator, estimates a stationary representation of the system's evolution. We then introduce the Koopman spectral density, a new frequency-domain object that extends the operator's properties to frequency domain, and use it to recover the underlying operator. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, and we apply the framework to estimate the connectivity of a real financial system.

A living organism's movement within a complex background can be distinguished from background features and anomalies by creating a set of computational models that mimic biologically unique characteristics. This approach helps our detector ignore non-relevant movements and focusing on the organism at the cost of slightly decreasing the ability to distinguish the organism from a highly similar background. We use a decision-tree of six feature detectors to characterize a living being's movement, though we acknowledge there are countless possible biological configurations. We test this general approach using still images of a walking insect, and show how our method can be adapted to detect specific organism types by modifying the underlying feature templates.

The project aims to further develop the RIMI algorithm, initially created by the research group, to expand its capabilities in order to accelerate the computation of certain tensor operations. The framework of the algorithm will be adapted to facilitate the efficient performance of a specific operation called t-Product. The operation in question involves the tensor product of a matrix with a vector, a operation that constitutes a fundamental component of various algorithms. Notably, this operation is a crucial building block for the implementation of Deep Learning models. The development of the RIMI algorithm will be demonstrated through numerical examples performed on a CPU and a GPU.

We've developed a topological Anderson conductor theory, which includes random binary perturbations, by drawing on topological insulator and random disorder theory. A 3D bulk model with a bulk energy gap and 2D surface states as its robust feature has been achieved by utilizing spin-orbit coupling and binary perturbations randomly distributed across space. The stability of the surface states was proven to be robust in the face of perturbation variations. Notably, in three-dimensional space, this model can serve as a foundation for constructing topological Anderson materials, filling a critical gap in topological material science.

This study focuses on a subset of genus-two curves over finite fields with a specific property: their j-invariants lie within a particular subset of the projective line. We categorize these curves into three distinct classes, determining the number of rational points they contain. Furthermore, we establish connections between these curves and a class of isogenies between genus-one curves equipped with pairings. Specifically, we demonstrate that isogenies induced by repeated application of a specific twist operation map genus-one curves with pairings to genus-one curves with pairings, essentially of the same type. This process results in a set of genus-one curves with pairings that can be parameterized by the original curve's parameters. We devise an explicit formula for one such curve, determining the coefficients needed for its construction. We also examine the relationship between the points defining the original curve and the coefficients of the new curve, facilitating the computation of endomorphisms of the new curve. Furthermore, we explore the effects of these isogenies on the points within the original curve, providing an expression for the points comprising the new curve. We validate our findings by comparing the results from these isogenies applied sequentially to the points of the original curve with the directly computed points of the new curve, employing example fields for demonstration purposes.

This presentation delves into the study of Higgs boson production within the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, focusing on variable SUSY mass spectra and focusing on on-shell Higgs physics. New detailed plots are provided, offering a comprehensive overview of the low-luminosity LHC and future high-energy experiments. A general scanning approach is compared to more refined analyses based on SUSY groupings, as well as exploratory investigations into rare decay modes of heavy Higgs bosons.

In multi-agent linear bandits with unknown environments, agents that cannot observe the global information must make decisions based on their local observations. This problem has several important applications, including personalization in recommendation systems and adaptive resource management. We study a decentralized approach where agents can ask the controller for recommendations based on their observations, but the controller does not know the individual environments. We develop two communication-efficient algorithms, each for a different setting. In the setting where environments are distinct, we present a decentralized learning scheme called "Distributed Contextual Linear Bandits via Controller as Trainer (DCLB-CAT)" with nearly optimal regret performance. In the setting where environments may overlap, we offer another algorithm called "Overlapping Contextual Linear Bandits via Controller as Trainer (OCLB-CAT)". Both of these algorithms have desirable regret properties, and their effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy optimization efficiency via inverse propensity score weighting. Building upon this, we offer an alternative perspective using the Lagrange multiplier, providing new insights into the equipping and embedding problems. Our results are further substantiated by a computational study.

Our study investigates how events are formed in 2.76 TeV lead-lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, particularly in relation to the elliptic pattern of particle distributions. Utilizing a highly detailed dataset with multiple subheadings, our research delves into several key aspects, starting with an examination of particle distributions' characteristics, followed by an analysis of particle formation phases' properties, and finally, an investigation into the connections between the elliptic pattern and collision side-effects.

This note calculates the extremal high-SNR GDoF gains of optimal power control over binary intensity modulation in interference networks, for any number of users with multiple-transmit and multiple-receive antennas. It shows that for $K$ users with $n_t$ transmit antennas and $n_r$ receive antennas, the maximum GDoF advantage of optimal power control is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ when $n_t \geq n_r$, and $\Theta(K)$ when $n_t < n_r$. The note also establishes an upper and lower bound on the extremal GDoF benefit of optimal power control, with respect to binary intensity modulation, for any number of users.

This study introduces a novel particle collision resolution method that simulates complex interactions between particles and fluid molecules in multiple time steps. By leveraging this approach, even the most intricate collisions can be accurately modeled, even when the time step is relatively long. A computational framework has been developed to implement this method, featuring adaptive resolution capabilities to balance simulation precision and efficiency. A model simulation with simplified conditions demonstrates the method's effectiveness, while a more comprehensive simulation, similar to those found in real-world applications, serves as a proof of concept.

This article presents new findings for the diophantine equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$, focusing on solutions where $a, b, $ and $n$ are whole numbers, and $n$ is greater than 2. Previously known solutions for this equation are analyzed, and a solution for $n=6$ is offered, along with the associated values for $a$ and $b$. Furthermore, the article discusses two relationships between $a$ and $b$, which are derived from the given equation and a seventh power. It is also shown that one of these relationships leads to a value of $7$ for either $a$ or $b$, which in turn generates a new parameter $k$, with $a$ equaling $k^3$ and $b$ equaling $7k^3$. The article then substitutes these values into the original equation, which simplifies to $k^6+7k^6=7^n$, and further rearranges to $k^{6}(1+7)=7^n$. It then observes that $n$ must be 6 to accommodate the factor $k^6$, which allows for possible values of $n$ to be examined within the range from 3 to 5, with corresponding values of $k$ also provided.

This research focuses on simulating a monopod locomotion on deformable ground to enhance the stability and efficiency of the device. By utilizing a simplified model, we analyzed the interplay between the ground's mechanical properties and the pod's movement. Our computational experiments revealed that our current design experiences limitations due to its linear design. Therefore, this study proposes an optimized linear model and suggests a curved foot shape to mitigate these constraints. Our results indicate that a curved foot reduces losses caused by slip-offs and valving, allowing for a 27% increase in speed and 20% improvement in stability.

Within the quark-diquark model, we've assessed the shape factors of mesons made from light quarks, whether leptons or gluons, by calculating their form factors using lattice QCD. Our study involved calculating the charge radii of mesons with various quark masses and different diquark interpolations. We found that the shape factors are largely independent of the quark mass and systematically depend on the diquark's nature, varying predictably based on the quark and diquark masses. Our findings are consistent with similar studies on heavy quarks. We also explored how the shape factors change for mesons composed of different quark and diquark combinations, offering a framework for calculating the radii of heavy mesons like charmed and beauty mesons.

Hierarchies within information systems, particularly taxonomies and ontologies, require a solid foundation for their bottommost nodes. These base nodes serve as the basis for deriving upper-level concepts through abstraction. Achieving this balance can be challenging, as it demands both extensive knowledge of lower-level specifics and a narrow focus on upper-level generalities. Current model-based approaches fail to address this issue, as they prioritize linear reasoning processes over complex relationships between high and low-level nodes. In response, this research introduces expandable description logic models that enable efficient reasoning about information system hierarchies. These models can calculate implied statements at both the upper and lower levels, ensuring consistency across the entire hierarchy. A real-world example from the medical domain demonstrates the efficacy of these models in accurately representing and inferring both high and low-level knowledge.

Quantum annealing within an uncertain interval can lead to varying success rates for solving combinatorial problems, ultimately affecting the quality of solutions obtained through quenching. This study examines the effects of systematic errors on quantum annealing's success rate and solution precision, using the precise cover problem as its model. We find that the distribution of success rates following an annealing protocol can be non-Gaussian, leading to a discussion on its implications, including the potential breakdown of Gaussian approximations that underlie many quantum annealing simulations.

Recent discoveries of the infinite-layer nickelate LNiO2, which exhibit similar properties to cuprates, have sparked interest in a new class of materials. Studies have found that infinite-layer nickelates display both strong correlation and direct optical transition, making them suitable for optical 2-band model simulations. Using a dynamical mean-field theory, researchers have created a model that simulates the optical properties of infinite-layer nickelates and have screened the free 2-band model using a localized view of the nickel ion. Contrary to expectations, they found that the on-site Coulomb repulsion can be significantly reduced due to screening, which was verified through calculations of the nickel ion's charge and orbital occupation. Additionally, reduced electron correlations were observed near the Fermi level, which could explain the infinite-layer nickelates' itinerant electronic nature. Furthermore, by adjusting the transfer integral, researchers were able to replicate the results from previous studies on cuprates and even infinite-layer nickelates themselves, thereby validating their model.

Researchers studied dense matter models with strange quarks and found that dense quark matter generally has a constant adiabatic index across a wide range of densities. However, when considering negative charged compact stars, a fluctuation in this index occurred, ultimately influencing the stars' sound speeds. A calculated sound speed spectrum led to defining a critical density, above which the adiabatic index drops, contributing to instability in the stars. This phenomenon was observed in models where stars are composed of rotating strange quark matter or meson-quark hybrid matter. A semi-analytical approach and numerical simulations using the TOV framework and a polytropic equation of state for dense matter revealed that the sound speed in hybrid stars deviates from the constant adiabatic index quark matter sound speed by less than 0.5, allowing this model to replicate various observational constraints. This study's findings also related the maximum mass of stable stars to the sound speed in quark matter, offering a clear, calculable standard for future observations of high-mass stars.

We have derived an exact formula to calculate the average number of particles in a quantum state's basis, utilizing a non-local bosonic Bogoliubov transformation with varying compression and shift parameters across different modes. These calculations lead to the formation of new quantum states with defined particle numbers in specific modes. The entropy of these states is found to follow an exponential decay when the compression parameter is below a certain threshold, the entanglement between modes also behaves differently based on the shift parameter. The calculation of average particle numbers enables us to define conditions for specific states with a minimum or maximum number of particles in particular modes. The proposed scenario can be applied to a variety of physical systems, including Josephson junctions, optical lattices, and spin-symmetric condensates.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases. Unlike the internal VSI triggered by a solid body, the external VSI is influenced by how quickly gases dissipate momentum and energy, making it difficult to explain observed dust buildup in outer disk regions. Our computer simulations demonstrate that even modest levels of gas dissipation can suppress the VSI, leading to enhanced dust accumulation in outer disk regions and shaping the appearance of these regions when observed under infrared light. Additionally, our findings also demonstrate that the VSI's behavior can be determined by a single parameter that combines factors like the rate of gas dissipates energy, the speed of rotational motion, and how quickly gases move vertically above one another. Notably, these results are consistent with previous studies of the VSI conducted without considering gas dissipation.

This research focuses on examining the Liouville theorem within a specific framework of manifolds with reduced Ricci curvature and constant scalar curvature. A crucial aspect of this study involves exploring the geometric consequences resulting from the absence of a boundedness property of a specific integral in these manifolds. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the Liouville theorem can be applied to establish the boundedness of the mentioned integral within these manifolds.

In multi-view 3D reconstruction, a model gathers data from various angles before combining it into a comprehensive 3D model. Current entrance modules in these models process input features from all views simultaneously, leading to an over-reliance on large sets of views. This limitation can result in subpar performance when there are only a few views available. To address this issue, we propose a dynamic entrance structure that adapts to the number of views being used. In this new setup, the entrance breaks down each view's features into segments before a global mean pooling process combines them. We tested this model on the NUADIS and 3D Ground Truth datasets, achieving superior performance compared to traditional entrance structures.

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are susceptible to post-Newtonian relativistic effects, especially in measurements of large scales. Similarity in observation patterns could mimic systematic errors. This paper calculates the impact of PPN $\gamma$ uncertainty on the results from future parallax measurements using a satellite observatory similar to Gaia, both in simulation environments and with actual Gaia data. It is evident that tighter constraints on $\gamma$ will be obtained from these measurements, with a predicted value of $\sigma_{\gamma} \approx 0.01$ based on anticipated measurement precision. This will significantly improve the overall PPN $\gamma$ estimation accuracy.

To improve commonsense questioning tasks like CommonsenseQA, which evaluate common sense knowledge, our proposed method fine-tunes language models for semantic connection. To assess this connection, we use the task's own data, without relying on external sources. Our approach, called FRC, first employs a rough search to narrow down the answer choice list, then refines the model to carefully choose the correct answer from the remaining options. To ensure the connection between answers is meaningful, we enforce a critical threshold on the model's careful choice's confidence score. Our results show that even a basic version of FRC, without additional training data, outperforms current benchmarks. Furthermore, when we incorporate more training data, FRC's performance continues to rise, surpassing current record holders.

Precise knowledge of cometary molecules is crucial for analyzing the thermal and photochemical evolution of particles within a comet's tail. A review of recent studies using the Herschel Space Observatory reveals a lack of data on ground-state energetic levels for certain oxygen-containing molecular cations, hindering a complete understanding of these molecules' behavior and composition of the comet's particles. Specifically, deficiencies in data exist for the magnitude of spin-orbit interactions in the cations of water, carbon dioxide, and carbon monoxide, which significantly affect both astrophysical and laboratory contexts. As a result, further observations are necessary to comprehensively grasp the photochemical and thermal processes influencing a comet's particles, and to validate certain laboratory-based models used to simulate post-comet impact charges within the tail.

In the context of a decentralized learning system where data is distributed across different locations and each contribution comes with a cost, we face a significant challenge in developing fair machine learning models that accurately represent all populations, taking into account imbalances in data availability. Here, we present a novel randomized approach to address these challenges in multi-class problems. First, we introduce a method to estimate diversity in data, quantifying the overlap between different populations. We then develop a stochastic flatform for federated learning, prioritizing visits to regions with unique data. The number of visits to each area is directly proportional to its diversity score. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method in multiple scenarios, showing notable improvements over existing fair learning techniques.

Research indicating the mental health challenges faced by prisoners has prompted many countries to implement compulsory psychological treatments within prisons. Yet, there's limited research examining the benefits of such interventions for this population. A new study examines the link between mandatory psychological treatments and prisoners' psychological well-being, considering various factors that might influence this relationship. It also explores the long-term effects of these programs on prisoners' mental health happiness, life satisfaction, and resilience after release from prison. A significant increase in prisoners' mental health happiness, life satisfaction, and resilience was found among those who completed the treatment program compared to those who did not. These positive outcomes persisted for up to three years following their release from prison. Notably, prisoners who underwent the treatment program showed improved psychological well-being compared to those who did not participate. Although certain prison characteristics were found to impact prisoners' mental health happiness, life satisfaction, and resilience, the study revealed that treatment programs can successfully improve the psychological well-being of incarcerated individuals. These results can be utilized by policymakers and corrections professionals to enhance the design and implementation of prison mental health programs and better address the mental health needs of this population.

In healthcare image segmentation, accurate annotation is crucial but often impractical or time-consuming to obtain for large datasets due to the expertise required and resulting time costs. This paper leverages less common techniques for validating medical image data, utilizing consistency regularization to enhance semi-supervised image segmentation. Specifically, we employ an image as the input and generate two segmentations from it using different transformations, then calculate the difference between these two segmentations to add to the loss function during training. This additional loss term encourages the network to produce consistent results when given the same image, thereby indirectly verifying that the network itself is functioning correctly. We applied this method to compare and contrast with more complex validation techniques and found it to be a cost-effective and simple yet highly competitive approach, surpassing or at the very least matching the performance of more sophisticated methods in various medical image segmentation tasks.

To measure the complexity of a quantum system's dynamics, the graph neural network approach is utilized in this study to create a simple graph that represents the system's time-dependent Hilbert space. By analyzing this graph over time, researchers can extract crucial information about the system's quantum chaos levels, as well as its quantum state and time-dependent Hamiltonian. A new metric called the "chaos vertex" is also introduced to characterize the direction of increasing chaos in the system's phase space. This method is particularly suitable for estimating the system's entropy production rate, which is a key indicator of chaos. To validate this approach, it is applied to both simple, non-chaotic models and those that exhibit quantum chaos, including the Dyson chamber model and the Jaynes-Cummings model subject to a periodic drive.

In the general case, estimating the parameters of a mixture requires knowing the individual parameters of its components. A new method, based on an extended likelihood ratio, allows for estimating the average parameter of a blend by analyzing the mixture itself, without requiring knowledge of the individual parameters of its components. This new method, however, requires that the components of the mixture have distinct properties and that their parameters change noticeably with changes in the mixture. This assessment method can be used to assess the representativeness of a sample, which is part of a larger population, by analyzing that sample alone. This paper presents the statistical theory behind this assessment method and provides practical applications related to sampling.

Knowledge tracing in online educational platforms has gained significant interest in recent years, with significant improvements in accuracy achieved through the application of deep learning techniques. As knowledge representation methods own their own distinct strengths and weaknesses, it is essential to carry out rigorous evaluations to validate their effectiveness in specific contexts. To facilitate such assessments, this study presents PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for examining the performance of deep learning-based knowledge tracing systems. PyKT enables researchers to systematically explore the implications of model parameters, learning theory, and data characteristics on knowledge representation and task performance. Furthermore, this study is characterized by the expression of concerns and potential research directions emerging from initial experiments conducted within the PyKT framework.

Let $\Omega$ be an open set in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and consider the space $H$ of functions that have derivatives up to order $k$ within $L^2(\Omega)$. When $\Omega$ is bounded or has a compact interior, it is known that the subset of functions in $H$ with compact support is the only subspace of functions in $H$ that forms a Hilbert algebra under the operator norm topology. In this paper, we prove that this result extends to a broader class of domains, specifically those with the property that they contain no lines or planes.

In complex mathematical proofs, having an automated reasoning tool is crucial for assisting in certain steps, but maintaining the automated evidence up-to-date can be challenging. To streamline this process, we propose an innovative way to incorporate multiple automated proofs using different SMT solvers and protocols. Our approach enables proof assistants to easily switch between different proof strategies and solvers, even if the underlying logic changes. To demonstrate the versatility of this method, we used Alethe to combine YX proofs for the Z3 solver and CVC3 solver, and showed that it is possible to switch from one solver to another with just a change in the proof strategy, not the proof itself.

In large-scale federated learning, participating nodes often have limited computational resources and cannot afford continuous data upload. This constricts nodes to perform model updates locally before contributing to the central model. However, current optimization methods typically rely on nodes having access to unconstrained gradient information. In reality, nodes may operate in a more controlled environment where gradient updates are constrained, making FedBuffSA particularly appealing due to its flexibility in handling unbounded gradients. In our work, we explore the theoretical stability properties of FedBuffSA when nodes have access to unconstrained gradients. Our results show that when nodes adhere to a specific data generation process, the central model exhibits optimal performance. Our simulations also demonstrate the efficacy of FedBuffSA in scenarios where nodes have access to unbounded gradients.

In large-scale ASR systems, introducing multi-task learning can facilitate the model in distinguishing similar-sounding words. Nonetheless, such models are typically more complex and require a significant amount of data. We present an alternative approach called RTD-ASR that reverses this paradigm by training a simpler model on a limited amount of data, first. This base model then serves as the starting point for more complex models trained on larger datasets. Our experiments demonstrate that RTD-ASR yields comparable results to state-of-the-art multi-task ASR models while significantly reducing model complexity and data requirements. Additionally, we explore ASR transfer across languages using RTD-ASR, leveraging limited amounts of target-language data to enhance the model's phonetic awareness, thereby improving zero-shot ASR performance on the target language. Our code is available at https://github.com/GoogleTLG/RTD-ASR.

To ensure safe and efficient navigation, marine robots need to consider the dynamic nature of their surroundings. In complex environments with multiple moving targets, navigation strategies are compromised if they don't account for target speeds and acceleration. This paper presents a novel method for learning the temporal variation of targets within the robot's perception field, using multiple Gaussian Process regressors to model target attributes and dynamic variation. A sparse representation is employed to limit the number of targets and their attributes, with a new algorithm developed to solve the resulting nonconvex optimization problem. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, with results showing it outperforms existing methods in various scenarios.

We employ a linearized General Relativity model to investigate self-gravitating fluid spheres comprised of two distinct fluids of varying densities, not necessitating density ratios less than a certain threshold. By bypassing the usual requirement for small total mass, we're able to explore a range of total masses while keeping the more massive component's density constant. Our method allows us to determine the stability criteria for these two-component systems by analyzing the rest mass and energy density contributions within the metric tensor. Our findings reveal that such a system is dynamically stable if its total energy is below the threshold of its critical value. Additionally, we determine the radius of the system and its equilibrium condition, further confirming its stability. Our approach also facilitates the derivation of an exact, non-linear stability criterion, which can be compared against the well-known, but less precise, Tohline's criterion. Our results apply not only to two-fluid systems but also to single-fluid spheres, provided the maximum density does not exceed the critical density.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based grammatical error rectification methods focus primarily on generating synthetic data to train models for low-resource languages. An alternative approach, known as source domain augmentation, involves utilizing high-resource languages to enhance models for resources with limited data. We delve into exploring this second strategy, specifically investigating whether transferring knowledge from one domain to another with only a limited number of examples can improve the accuracy of error correction models. To address this, we employ a pointer-network based explicit reconstruction of the target sentence, integrated with a domain transfer framework that leverages stylistic differences between domains. To determine the optimal number of reference sentences for training style-invariant representations, we utilize a fixed number of reference sentences across all domains. Our proposed method, known as Meta-GERC, utilizes multi-task learning to simultaneously learn both domain-specific and style-invariant representations. Experimental evaluations on the native language identification task demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model, specifically with respect to zero-shot and few-shot domain transfer. Furthermore, we investigate the domains for which transfer is successful, finding that our method yields enhanced results when transferring from domains with significantly more data.

The task of allocating precious items to self-interested individuals, where the value each person places on an item is unknown, is a classic challenge. We examine two fair distribution objectives, maximizing the total value of items and ensuring that each person gets a similar total value, and explore their relationship in the context of item allocations. We then investigate two scenarios, one where items are interchangeable and another where they are not, and provide a clear understanding of pure Nash equilibria for both scenarios and both mentioned objectives. When items are distinct and there are multiple agents, we identify a key observation that only combinatorial auctions without frugality properties have pure Nash equilibria that respect equality, whereas all other cases ensure fairness through a more general property called fractional stability. When items are interchangeable, we show there are pure Nash equilibria that respect equality, as well as those that respect proportionality, and these two equilibria classes are distinct, one of them being supported by fractional stability, and the other by equality, with one class containing the other.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in its central region.
An exceptionally long rotation period of 84 hours has been observed in UGC 8839, a record for a spiral galaxy.
High-resolution radio observations revealed a compact, edgeless HII region only in the galactic center, suggesting that the absence of star formation in the outer regions could be attributed to lack of gas.
An extremely low level of stellar evolution was observed, with no globular star clusters evident outside the central bulge.
The galaxy exhibits no signs of interaction with its neighboring galaxies, and its low mass (less than 1.4 times 10 to the power of 9 solar masses) suggests a slow rate of gas consumption.
Consequently, the galaxy is thought to be in a stable, quiescent state, with the central region's higher density causing the rotating disk to become unstable at 84 hours.

Lattice QCD data for various two-current correlations in the pion have been analyzed to derive new relations that incorporate momentum dependence. Our study leverages recent advancements in extracting matrix elements from lattice simulations, specifically two-current matrix elements typically required in relativistic dissociation processes. Furthermore, we clarify the connection between standard light-cone functions and their corresponding average behavior. The predicted average behaviors were compared with previously computed pion distributions in leptoproduction and relativistic dissociation processes, demonstrating that the predicted effects are too small to be resolved with current experimental capabilities.

Detailed monitoring of the light collected from XX Cha during 2013-2014 using the PACO camera at the 1.4m CCCD telescope revealed unusual variations in accretion rates. Distinguishing between external interstellar dust and dust within the disk, we found an increased amount of dust inside the disk, which is likely responsible for the observed high accretion rates. If this is the case, then XX Cha represents a unique phase where accretion rates remain high during a known pause in stellar accretion, occurring about 0.1 AU from the star. This phenomenon may be caused by a massive disk particle falling towards the star. Analyzing more data from XX Cha over the next few years is essential to fully comprehend this phenomenon and its potential impact on the Alfvén wave theory.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
safety-critical systems like self-driving cars and human-robot collaborations.
Reinforcement learning models are typically evaluated based on expected future
returns, but this approach can lead to generalization issues when applied to
new, unseen situations. To address this challenge, we propose a new method for
learning from positive past experiences of multiple interacting agents. Our
algorithm, called Positive Multi-Agent Policy Learning (PMAPL), can handle a
large number of agents efficiently, even in challenging generalization scenarios.
We complement our approach with a study on the conditions under which our
algorithm produces models that generalize well, drawing on connections to low-
dimensional extrapolation. When compared to existing multi-agent learning
techniques, our proposed method achieves superior performance in various rigorous
tests of generalization ability. Our code is available at https://github.com/...
{pmapplearn}.

We developed a novel approach for aligning MV images obtained from different planes. This method leverages Convolutional Neural Architectures, specifically U-Net and Dense U-Net, to fuse 2D and 3D images. A simple post-processing technique is employed to refine the aligned images. Our evaluation used synthetic 2D projections created from 3D images, aligning 2D images with their corresponding 3D data plane. We also investigated plane classification for 3D images. Our results show that the U-Net and Dense U-Net architectures can classify planes accurately, with an average accuracy of 97.5% and 96% respectively. Additionally, we evaluated our image alignment technique using synthetic and real-world data, obtaining alpha diversity of 0.02 and 0.09 for U-Net and Dense U-Net, and beta diversity of 0.013 and 0.052 for U-Net and Dense U-Net, respectively.

We demonstrate that single-particle entanglement, regardless of its degree, gives rise to nonlocal effects between two distant systems, referencing a scenario where the outcome of measuring a quantity on one system instantly affects the result of measuring another quantity on the other system, located in a different place. This effect occurs with an uncorrelated state, yet it's missing in unentangled, two-particle states. Our study reveals that the average amount of entanglement per system isn't an appropriate measure for predicting the magnitude of these nonlocal effects. Instead, we use the Chernoff distance to measure the difference between the outcome distributions of the two systems, showing that the distance between the outcome distributions of the two systems is always non-zero when the state is entangled, whereas the average entanglement per system can be arbitrarily small. We also examine the relationship between the Chernoff distance and the average entanglement per system, concluding that there is an infinite disparity between their rate-of-convergence-to-zero values.

The integration of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) technology within the educational sector is presenting significant challenges in terms of security, privacy, and trustworthiness. As the existing infrastructure is not sufficiently advanced to meet these demands, there's a growing interest in a federated education system for IoV. This system could provide a platform for secure, private, and trustworthy knowledge sharing and exchange. To understand the current state of these innovative technologies, this paper conducts an in-depth review of the scientific literature on blockchain-based, federated education systems for IoV. With the aim of identifying areas that require further research, the study delves into the technical aspects, challenges, and security-related concerns of these systems.

V392 Persei, a well-known small nova from 2018, has been observed in various spectral ranges since its revival in 2019.  V392 Persei's revival showed distinctive characteristics including prolonged emission at multiple wavelengths for nearly three years.  Observations from ROSAT, X-ray Telescope, Swift, Chandra, and NuSTAR revealed that the nova system is highly interactive, with evidence of a rapidly spinning black hole of 0.32 solar masses and a 5.4 day orbital period around it.  V392 Persei can be found among the smallest known novae that experience multiple outbursts and exhibit extreme gamma-ray brightness.  A comparison of its pre-and post-eruption data revealed that the 2018 nova eruption significantly increased the system's luminosity, resulting in its transition from an isolated black hole to a persistent accretion system.  V392 Persei, with its exceptional characteristics, is an extraordinary object that challenges current theoretical models.

In large FDD systems, developing precoders and encoders and encoding feedback information can be challenging due to their substantial computational cost. This study leverages Gaussian mixture modeling (GMM) to create codebooks used for feedback encoding, reducing encoding costs. Additionally, a low-complexity method is proposed for precoder and encoder development utilizing only the mean and covariance of GMM components, further minimizing computational requirements. Simulations demonstrate the proposed approach outperforms existing methods.

A type of sturdy, nonequilibrium interface was recently discovered in two-dimensional models, characterized by a fixed location of the interface and rolling waves of different species flanking it. In the three-dimensional Hofstadter model, we found that sturdy interfaces can occur along the edges of a cubic lattice, provided that certain conditions are met regarding flux quanta and filling. Notably, these interfaces can be both non-equilibrium and two-dimensional in their own right. Our calculations indicate that sturdy interfaces can resist disturbances, and that the behavior of particles in this system can be understood using effective one-dimensional models.

The rate of change of mass flow through event horizons during black hole formation was initially subject to uncertainty, but Bondi theory provides a framework for studying this phenomenon. Initially, research focused solely on the rate of change of mass, but later it was realized that the rate of change of mass and its associated conserved charge, such as magnetic flux, also need to be considered. The rate of change of mass can differ from its flux to the horizon by a factor equal to the surface area of the horizon. This disparity can result in mass escaping the horizon despite a negative mass flux to the horizon. A study of binary neutron star mergers, specifically GW170817, provides a specific measure of this effect. It shows that even at low accretion rates, the Bondi mass increase rate is likely minimal, limiting the rate of mass increase to less than 10% of the rate of accretion, or in other words, at least 90% of the accreted mass gets converted into energy rather than being added to the black hole mass.

We have made observations of the galaxy's core with infrared and radio waves, 
and used a computational model to study the formation and evolution of stars 
in these core regions. Based on our analysis, even the most massive stars that 
form in these regions do not have enough mass to produce gravitational waves from 
merging black holes, a key feature of some current gravitational wave detections. 
However, we do expect to find waves from another type of gravitational event - 
neutron stars and black stars (a type of dead star formed from a white dwarf that 
has swollen to an enormous size). These predictions vary depending on the level 
of gas that fills the space between stars and how massive the most prolific 
star-makers are, but we estimate there should be approximately 400 of these 
events recorded by the LIGO and Virgo gravitational wave detectors per century, 
with the most powerful signals likely to be found in the Milky Way and the Andromeda 
galaxy.

In multi-carrier wireless communications, combining different subbands can improve physical layer security by balancing throughput and confidentiality. This study focuses on an end-to-end cooperative communication system using single-source and single-receiver architecture. An optimized method for dividing subbands is proposed, prioritizing those with the best signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) to ensure secure data transfer. A threshold-based stopping criterion is established to limit the number of subbands created through successive refinement, striking a balance between security and throughput. Simulation results confirm that our proposed scheme outperforms existing methods in terms of throughput and confidentiality.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based game platforms is their slow speed, topping out at around 300 moves per second, which hampers the ability to conduct rigorous testing for high-capability agents.
In response to this challenge, we present TextWorldExpress, a groundbreaking platform that accelerates text games by an incredible 3,000 times, allowing for an astonishing one million moves per second.
This extraordinary speed is achieved through a novel hybrid approach that combines symbolic reinforcement learning with a general-purpose computing engine, leveraging multiple CPU cores and a separate virtual machine to execute actions and observe responses. 
The resulting platform exhibits flawless scalability, consistently demonstrating linear performance improvements in sync with enhancements in hardware capabilities. 
Our evaluation methods for evaluating TextWorldExpress's performance showcase its incredible speed, whereas quality assessments highlight areas for improvement. 
TextWorldExpress is available to the public as an open-source tool, suitable for use in large-scale text-based games.

In order to significantly reduce power consumption in large-scale deep learning models for continuous video recognition, we propose an innovative co-design approach that synchronizes algorithmic advancements with hardware optimization. Our algorithmic contribution involves using long short-term memory (LSTM) models, which effectively capture temporal dependencies, and we further develop an energy-efficient LSTM architecture based on hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition (HTTD). From the hardware perspective, we designed a customized LSTM core and implemented it using 1,052 programmable logic elements (PLEs) on an FPGA. Our co-designed framework, which utilizes a 4x 128-bit data path, can process 12 frames per second for the video identification task. Our experiments showed that the proposed HTTD model achieved a top-1 accuracy of 83.7% for the LISA dataset and 73.6% for the KHRA dataset. In comparison to the conventional LSTM model, our HTTD model exhibited a 50x reduction in multiplication operations and a 7x decrease in memory usage.

The average energy density within black holes is the same regardless of what type of matter is dropped into them, a finding based on general relativity. If we consider a quantum field theory, a specific property called the "weak energy condition" is met when the average energy density generated by a particular field in the vicinity of a point is non-negative. When the energy condition is examined in both its weak and strong forms within the context of conformal field theories, a notable discrepancy emerges. The strong energy condition is consistently violated in these theories, whereas the weak energy condition is observed only at specific points, particularly when the stress tensor is conformally invariant. The strong energy condition's consistent violation and the weak energy condition's violation in the infrared regime serve as the foundation for an unconfirmed hypothesis known as the "Feeble Gravity Conjecture." Notably, the conjecture has been supported by both 2D and 4D CFT analyses. The weak energy condition's violation is further accentuated by the predicted violation of the conformal covariance of the average stress tensor's expectation value in the infrared regime. The Feeble Gravity Conjecture's components, including the predicted violation of the conformal covariance and the anticipated behavior of the entropy of black holes, can be found in the paper's appendix.

Given a Noetherian local ring R whose maximal ideal m is F-rational, we establish that a parameter h of R is F-regular if and only if the compact Hilbert function H_R/h diminishes polynomially. Additionally, in the case where depth R equals its dimension, this condition is equivalent to the F-rational property of R being equivalent to the property that H_R/h is polynomially dimened.

In recent years, there has been growing interest in using auxiliary services to mitigate market power in electricity markets. However, research in this field is largely theoretical and lacks empirical support. This study aims to fill this gap by examining auxiliary services procurement policies in the context of wholesale electricity markets, specifically in Australia and the United States, using case studies of three regions each. Although these studies reveal insights into industry practices, they also highlight limitations and potential negative consequences of current policies, such as exaggerated price responses and market instability. Further, it becomes clear that industry participants prioritize strategic behavior over truthful reporting of generation costs. Consequently, this research suggests that cost reflection is not a necessary condition for auxiliary services procurement, and policymakers should consider alternative methods for reducing market manipulation, such as increasing information disclosure, implementing robust pricing mechanisms, and designing better separation protocols.

For a given complex plane, we investigate the behavior of the set defined by the union of the graphs made by applying a polynomial to one component and another polynomial to the other component, followed by repeated iterations of this process. We first determine the conditions under which this set is bounded within the plane. Furthermore, we establish that if both polynomials are of degree greater than one, this set will fill the plane. Additionally, we provide a comparative analysis of the interior of the set after an even number of iterations and the exterior of the set after an odd number of iterations.

Saturn's northern hexagon, an exceptionally straight-sided storm pattern, has been observed to evolve in response to changing temperatures and atmospheric conditions. Recently, a unique hexagonal shape appeared in Saturn's northern atmosphere, surrounding the developing polar vortex that marks the beginning of Saturn's summer in the northern hemisphere. This newly formed hexagon is distinct from the long-standing hexagon located further south, and it is thought to be caused by the interaction of strong winds with Earth-sized polar vortices that are beginning to form. Notably, this phenomenon provides scientists with a rare opportunity to study the formation of Saturn's northern polar vortex, which has not been observed before.

This research tackles a part of Cauchy problem for the nonlinear Schrödinger equation where solutions are examined outside a convex wall. Both conservative and dissipative cases are studied. For the conservative case, with a small initial disturbance, we show how solutions behave in the region far from the wall, particularly far from any point of the wall where the solution's amplitude diminishes in accordance with a specific, predetermined pattern. In the dissipative case, with another type of initial conditions, we demonstrate how solutions behave in the region far from the wall, with their amplitude decreasing in accordance with a different, predetermined pattern. Both patterns occur over time periods that grow in proportion to certain square root functions of time.

We demonstrate the existence of a locally effective algorithm to decide whether a given polynomial expression can be part of a polynomial set defining a subset of a variety in positive characteristic.

We demonstrate how a graded collection's polarization property can be characterized in terms of dual collections and Yoneda products. This characterization is shown to be equivalent to the condition that the collection's underlying connections map to zero under the natural differentiation process. Furthermore, this criterion is found to be necessary and sufficient to ensure the polarization of both linear and quadratic collections within a specific context.
This informal note explains the precise measure construction proposed by K. Coradiu, based on the idea of orbital integrals.

Our proposed experiment involves using resonant x-ray scattering to accomplish nuclear phase recovery spectroscopy on the iron atom within iron chalcogenides. Due to the nearly identical masses of iron's two isotopes, the coherent phonon mode's phase is expected to remain constant over time, allowing for the isolation of oscillator strengths through phase-recovery spectroscopy. Conversely, the two isotopes will have a notable mass difference in the two-phonon combination modes, leading to a phase that can be influenced by the phonon mode and thus provide insight into the phonon mode's frequency, damping, and start-of-life oscillatory behavior. This approach can be realized using a single x-ray pulse and static magnetic fields, and we have conducted numerical simulations to demonstrate the feasibility of this method for recovering isoscalar magnetic form factor functions, which can also facilitate the investigation of primary phonon modes in other materials.

This research introduces a new numerical approach, known as the hybrid combined finite volume-method, to simulate single-phase Darcy flow within porous media featuring discrete fractures. These fractures are characterized by distinct, high-kappa regions intermingled with the surrounding low-kappa medium. A combined approach is taken where the finite volume method is applied to model the porous media, whereas the finite element technique is used to model the fractures. A special interface technique is developed to connect the fractures with the surrounding media. A penalty function is employed to ensure continuity across the interface. Numerical experiments were conducted to evaluate the accuracy and efficiency of this technique, and it was found to provide reliable and precise results even with varying fracture media configurations.

Vandenberghe and Daudin (2020) examined the performance of Bayes factor methods in identifying the true model component, and our present study explores different workflow approaches for calculating Bayes factors. We utilized both simulated and real-world datasets to evaluate our results, concluding that the sequential application of Metropolis-Hastings and Laplace Metropolis Estimators produces the best overall results, although other methods also show promise. We open-source our BayesFactorR R package, which includes example usage for both simulated and real data.

In genres like academic and technical writing, writers use various discourse indicators to manage structure and convey complex information, yet the functions that different indicators serve are often contentious among researchers. This dispute is reflected in the many classifications proposed for these indicators, yet the studies supporting these categories often rely on limited, biased evidence. To address this issue, we present a method for objectively identifying categories based on the functions that discourse indicators serve, using data from clear writing genres. Our approach incorporates artificial intelligence in the form of machine learning algorithms and a custom-designed interface for categorization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to 12 features proposed by Bannard and McCarthy (2004), resulting in a more nuanced understanding of the relationships between categories and the functions that discourse indicators serve. We have made DiscSense available online for users to examine the proposed categories for themselves.

We have investigated a general matrix optimization problem under the assumption of a fixed-rank positive semidefinite matrix variable. To the best of our knowledge, this problem has not been studied before. We have demonstrated that when the dimension of the matrix is two, this problem is solvable using a second-order Riemannian steepest descent method. However, for matrices of any fixed rank greater than two, we have found that this problem does not have a non-singularity property when using a certain norm. Nevertheless, we have established a framework to characterize the non-singularity property in a more general context. Moreover, we have shown that a wide range of well-known matrix optimization problems can be viewed as specific cases of this general problem, and provided a worldwide landscape analysis for several well-known matrix optimization problems. Notably, these include the Burer-Monteiro approach to solving large-scale semidefinite programming problems, as well as several other well-known matrix optimization problems.

A graph's edge-tinting involves assigning different colors to its edges based on a set of given colors, ensuring that similar vertices have distinct colors. This problem has various equivalent formulations, making it a significant topic of study. Recently, a study was conducted to examine all non-homogeneous cubic bipartite graphs with regard to their ability to withstand edge-tinting that could use three or more colors. This process uncovered a robust edge-tinting structure applicable to many graphs, including those that require three colors, suggesting a new approach to determining if a graph can use three colors. However, further investigation revealed that a specific graph, the Frucht-Grotz graph, cannot be efficiently represented using this structure, implying that there is a more complex way to define such a structure.

To analyze the effectiveness of coevolutionary algorithms in achieving Nash Equilibrium in symmetric Cournot games, we utilized two genetic methods: traditional GA and $\epsilon$-GA. Our research revealed that $\epsilon$-GA outperformed GA in reaching the Nash Equilibrium, with the majority of populations converging to the optimal state within a relatively short period of time. In contrast, the population converged at a slower rate using the standard GA approach. Our findings also indicated that even at equilibrium, the population exhibited a certain degree of variation when using the $\epsilon$-GA algorithm.

Consider a weighted directed graph D with n vertices, denoted as V(D), and let I(D) be the toric ideal associated with D. We establish that I(D)/I(D)_2 has a specific property: it does not contain exponents e_1, e_2, e_3 in $\mathbb{N}^3$ that satisfy the condition e_1+e_2+e_3=3 if and only if there are three directed paths in D with distinct start and end vertices. Additionally, we provide an alternative characterization of this property and show it is equivalent to a weaker condition related to I(D)/I(D)_2 being generated by quadratic polynomials.

Convolutional neural networks are susceptible to overflows caused by hardware intensity imprecisions, specifically due to inaccurate multiplier results. To address this issue, researchers have proposed various quantification methods that ensure CNNs can function reliably, even with limited precision hardware. These proposals often assume that the hardware operates according to specified parameters, which is not always the case. In contrast, our approach, Activation Range Monitoring (ARM), focuses on identifying safe operating ranges for each convolutional layer, regardless of the underlying hardware. By doing so, we build a security case ensuring that layer outputs remain within valid ranges, thereby preventing overflows and ensuring accurate results. To demonstrate ARM's effectiveness, we applied this approach to a real-world scenario involving MNIST with limited precision hardware.

Building upon the foundation of Jordanian twists, we have derived a generalized version. The generalized version, modified in the $r$-symmetrized format, meets the criteria for a Lie algebra gauge invariant. Additionally, the generalized version can be further developed to accommodate both the $r$-symmetrized and the full Lie algebra gauge invariants.

This study introduces a novel approach to create a unified semantic framework for multiple languages using word embeddings. Unlike existing methods that focus on combining different languages' embeddings, our approach leverages clustering and word embedding techniques to create separate, yet equivalent, representations for each language. We then align these representations by ensuring corresponding clusters in different languages have similar distribution patterns. Our results show that this method yields superior performance compared to current techniques, particularly in classification tasks. Moreover, this approach results in improved and consistent performance across different languages, as demonstrated by our experiments using both small and large data sets.

The initial production of pions, kaons, protons, and phi mesons has been studied in Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV using the ALICE detector at the LHC. Particle transverse momentum spectra were measured for the most central collisions (0-10% most central) across a range of transverse momentum from 0.2 to 5 GeV by the ALICE multiplicity selector and charge-alice detector. The measured spectra were compared to the ELISA fluid dynamical model, the TRENTO transport model, and the PYTHIA 8 event generator. The elliptical and radial flow patterns were extracted from the measured spectra using a four-parameter fit model. The magnitude of elliptical flow was found to be similar to that in Pb-Pb collisions at the same energy, whereas the radial flow was greater than in Pb-Pb collisions. The ratio of spectra for different species was found to be independent of transverse momentum. The ratio of kaon to pion spectra was found to be the same as in Pb-Pb collisions. In late October 2019, violent protests erupted in Chile, claiming numerous lives and causing extensive property damage. This research seeks to explore the early stages of the uprising from a quantitative perspective. By analyzing official statistics and a sample of social media data, we examined the spread of extreme violence throughout the country. Using a non-global SIR model as a framework, we simulated the protests' progression and identified several key patterns and values, including the average time it took for extreme violence to spread to neighboring regions, its rate of adoption in individual areas, and the overall number of regions it affected. We also explored how these values impacted the model's predictions and conducted a series of sensitivity tests to understand their significance. Further analysis revealed that the model overestimated the total number of regions affected by extreme violence but accurately predicted the overall timeline of the protests. We concluded that a simulation period of 12 days provided the most realistic representation of the protests' progression and course.

This research develops an innovative method for addressing the consistency issue for regular expression inequalities, extending the concept to include those with additional constraints. Our analysis reveals that determining if an inequality is consistent is equivalent to determining if a specific type of regular expression, created by manipulating the inequality, contains no meaningful patterns. Our approach creates such a detector using a combination of regular expression intersection and concatenation, as well as a technique for eliminating unnecessary patterns. Specifically, we developed a way to eliminate unnecessary patterns using a form of regular expression resolution, and our results include a decision-making framework for consistency by employing this process.

In this research, we integrated an external memory attention mechanism within our VIO framework to enhance navigation accuracy, as we found that optimizing the memory weights directly didn't yield significant improvements. To overcome this limitation, we modified the memory weights to be learned through backpropagation, resulting in a more efficient model that achieved state-of-the-art performance on the TUM VI dataset, surpassing the current record by 9%.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework for examining the next generation of Weyl semimetals, characterized by a "square root" that describes a linear operator in (3D) space, transforming nonlinearly in time and space. Our framework allows us to classify all possible types of these novel quantum states, and we can predict distinctive signatures in energy spectra and spin polarization patterns emitted in experiments. Furthermore, we discovered that some of these 3D Weyl semimetals can exhibit both all-around and one-dimensional behaviors simultaneously, known as "parent" and "child" types respectively, with distinct distinguishing features. Our theoretical model is underpinned by non-linear Schrödinger equations, which generate a vast array of 1D "child" Weyl semimetals from their 3D "parent" counterparts, offering a groundbreaking means of controlling and creating these exotic states experimentally.

This study presents numerical solutions to the electrical conductivity data completion problem, based on Maxwell's equations, with synthetic data. A semi-discrete scheme for the QR technique yields stable performance. Key factors such as time stepping, mesh size, and smoothing intensity are optimized to achieve precise results. A comparative analysis of different numerical methods for solving the nonlinear system reveals the effectiveness of Newton's method. A solution validity time frame is identified, and the impact of different time frames on solution accuracy is examined. A Lagrange multiplier approach is alternative to the Clausse-Gougaaud method but yields similar results.

In the context of information dissemination within complex networks, where entities may possess varying levels of knowledge, a key challenge arises from lacking clear indicators of an entity's prior knowledge. This lack of information hinders efficient learning methods. This paper addresses this challenge by developing two novel approaches: one calculates prior knowledge based on entity behavior, drawing from game theory, while the other draws from game theory to create a robust method for learning. Both of these methods were tested and proven effective through simulations conducted on multiple network types.

We analyze the rank growth of elliptic curves from rational numbers to quartic extensions in the Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$, and investigate how rank development is affected by the presence of ramification and non-abelian Galois action. Specifically, under certain conditions, we establish the rank development for a subset of elliptic curves with minimal ramification, showing that it contributes to the evidence for Rank:Bound in the $S_4$ case and provides a lower bound for the rank development in the $A_4$ case.

A crucial boundary, the quantum null energy condition (QNEC), is derived from the quantum complexity, yielding a lower bound for entanglement's rate of change in relation to its variation in a specific direction. This condition has been rigorously proven in certain models but remains speculative when applied to all situations and systems. To examine the validity of this condition in general, we consider it in holographic violations where the entanglement's rate of change can exceed its gradient, providing a clear indication of the limitations this condition must observe. Furthermore, we analyze the entanglement's rate of change during violations, investigating how it behaves in different situations, and determine the criteria under which the QNEC is valid, thereby clarifying its scope of application.

We have derived the minimum time required for two distinct quantum states to become distinguishable under accurate measurements, taking into consideration various unitary time evolutions in a two-level system. Our analysis shows that the minimum time can differ significantly, varying between half a multiple of a fundamental time period and a full multiple of the same period. The distinction is attributed to the system's dynamics, which can be classified into three types, each with distinct characteristics, and is reflected in the structure of the difference between the identity matrix and the evolution operator. Our study also reveals that the minimum time required can differ significantly when the system dynamics changes, offering a lower bound on the distinctiveness time that remains valid across different time evolutions.

This research develops an expression to calculate the H^1 norm of a specific interpolation operator used to translate functions from the space H^1 to the space C^1. This operator, denoted by I, takes a function f within the space H^1 and produces the function f applied to the operator I, which results in a continuous derivative equivalent to the original derivative of f. A formula to calculate the norm of I is derived, along with an inductive proof demonstrating its validity for n-dimensional Euclidean space.

Superconducting quantum circuits are being closely examined for their potential to tackle quantum computation challenges. However, the presence of both pure state pure loss and pure state pure dephasing ketos dissipation hinders their development. To better understand these phenomena, researchers are studying superconducting Josephson junctions that make up these circuits. This study involves investigating the terahertz dielectric loss and ensembles of quantum fluctuations in superconducting junctions using a terahertz microscope and scanning tunneling microscopy. It is evident that dielectric loss can be significantly reduced by heating junctions to just above their critical temperature, and that loss occurs at or near the junctions themselves, not in the surrounding material. Furthermore, this research reveals that the average fluctuation energy of Josephson junctions is directly related to their dielectric loss, and that this energy could be an important factor in determining junction's stability within a quantum coil.

This study delves into the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how solar energy, chemical reactions, and plate tectonics influenced its development over 3.8 billion years. A numerical model simulated the atmosphere's evolution from its early stages until the present, considering various geological processes, chemical interactions, and the effects of abiotic organic compounds on cloud composition. Notably, our results suggest that Venus's atmosphere experienced a critical period around 3.5 billion years ago, characterized by the sudden release of methane and associated cloud layer changes. This event's possible causes are explored, with scenarios including the sudden onset of oxygen-producing photosynthesis, the emergence of life, and alternative non-biological explanations.

Point processes that follow a nonlinear Hawkes model exhibit self-sustaining cycles and explosive behavior in response to external influences. To study these processes dynamically, we've developed a linearized Bayesian approach to estimate the parameters of nonlinear Hawkes models in a time-varying setting. By assuming that the intensity function is constant and known, we estimated the time-varying characteristics of a point process's driver process, which under mild conditions, allows us to recover the underlying parameters of the nonlinear model. Our method enables us to assess the stability of the process, identify sources of the process, and quantify the influence of these sources, as well as provide confidence intervals for these estimates.

Based on an approximate solution to the nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation, along with particle-in-cell and full-spectrum simulated radiation, we've investigated how a strong laser beam interacts with a magnetized plasma. Specifically, we've examined the effects it has on an electron beam's polarization properties and a possible mechanism for plasma wave enhancement. Our simulations revealed that a high-power laser beam can achieve near-total polarization conversion within a single pass through the magnetized plasma. Furthermore, when a plasma wave is taken into account, we found that another polarization component can emerge, and that this component can become dominant over a longer distance. Our study enforces the significance of considering the influence of plasma waves when studying the interaction between a high-power laser beam and an electron beam.

Re-examining radiative corrections to $K^+ \to \tau^+ \tau^- \gamma$ decay facilitates a more precise determination of the tau electric dipole moment. Previous studies have focused on this effect within the Standard Model, yet it has been overlooked that the corrected amplitude also influences the $CP$ asymmetry in $K_\mathrm{L} \to \pi^0 \gamma \gamma$. By re-analyzing this process, a more comprehensive understanding of $CP$ violation in the neutral kaon system can be gained. Moreover, this study reveals that the $CP$ asymmetry in $K_\mathrm{e4}$ decay is unrelated to the tau electric dipole moment. A new estimate of the tau's electric dipole strength yields $|d_\tau| < 4.7 \times 10^{-19}$ e.cm, with an improvement of 30%. This limit also applies to the magnetic moment of the tau, given its minimal impact on $K^+ \to \tau^+ \tau^- \gamma$ decay.

Quantum error correction is a critical function to maintain reliable quantum computations. Continuous-variable (CV) systems offer a versatile platform for implementing error correction protocols. This study focuses on a specific error model, where a rank-one measurement error is applied to a two-mode state, and we aim to enhance the error correction decoding process. Initially, the error can be identified using a standard approach, which classifies it as a displacement or a beam splitter error. To improve the decoding, we employ phase space reconstruction to analyze the two-mode state. This analysis enables us to characterize the error as belonging to one of three categories: (1) a displacement error, (2) a beam splitter error, or (3) a combined error consisting of both displacement and beam splitter components. The combined error scenario can be corrected by performing a Gaussian operation that combines displacement and beam splitter transformations. We determine the optimal threshold for distinguishing between the combined error and the other two error types, above which the combined error can be corrected with a successful probability of one. Moreover, we provide an executable code in MATLAB to demonstrate our enhanced decoding process through numerical simulations.

Building upon prior work by \cite{Ferrara:1992a}, the stress tensor of a CFT$_2$ state is re-expressed in AdS$_3$ coordinates, yielding a rotating cone whose volume is proportional to the state's 4d conformal charge. When this state includes a single primary operator with spin $s$, the cone transforms into a conical shape with $s$ rotational symmetries. The resulting stress tensor is then matched to the symmetric traceless tensor operator in CFT$_2$, establishing a direct relationship between the operator's conformal covariance and the resulting AdS$_3$ geometry. The proposed stress tensor expression is then confirmed to satisfy the conformal algebra, with the resulting Fierz-Pauli differential equations being solved to determine the exponentials of the AdS$_3$ coordinates, which define the operator's support within AdS$_3$. The proposed expression for the stress tensor is then demonstrated to be equivalent to the existing description based on lightcone coordinates. The proposed stress tensor expression is finally utilized to determine the geometric properties of rotating string endpoints in AdS$_3$, with the proposed expression being shown to describe a sphere rather than a cone.
